Chapter 13: Culture, Section 1: Language, Subversion

We learn in kindergarten that our earliest learned words have shades of meaning, and other words are used to express the more severe definitions. English is constructed this way so we can differentiate these shades and apply them where appropriate. Gradation is the difference between sad and dejected. ‘Sad’ and ‘dejected’ share a core meaning, but they have functional differences. It’s also the difference between annoyed and furious, and between linguistic relativity and linguistic determinism. As you can see from the last pair of terms, gradation applies to philosophical and political concepts. There are two ways by which a language can be subverted:

  1. Overload a language with frivolous complexity. The lexicon of the “social justice” crowd achieves this by inventing out of whole cloth words and phrases that represent concepts key to their ideology, and which insulate their followers from criticism. As with any other word, these invented words are vehicles to communicate their ideology’s concepts. The new words end up clashing with preexisting words in the language and creating confusion as to the gradation they represent. When they appropriate an existing word–giving it a new “definition”–its traditional interpretation clashes with their intent, thanks to the new words’ artificial–and erroneous–construction.
  2. Strip a language of its complexity. In this method, the existence of gradation between words is the target, not the goal. Altering gradation concomitantly alters the range of expression made possible by the language. This is particularly true of words that are philosophical or political in nature.

Have you ever been in a situation in which you were working with a specific word–any word–at such length or with such repetition that the word no longer “felt” to you like it had any meaning, or that it was even a “real” word at all? Take ‘comb,’ for instance. Comb. Comb comb. Comb comb comb comb comb. He combed a comb of honey. See, it doesn’t look like a “real” word anymore. Overuse can warp our perception of anything, not just words. What about a word the media loves to use, such as “blasted.” That’s a powerful word. It brings to mind connotations of weaponry–bombs, guns, and the like–and a certain amount of force, greater than the kind a human could normally exert through his own muscles. One wouldn’t say, “He blasted through the jungle”–more likely would be said, “He navigated through the jungle” or even “He tore through the jungle” if you wanted to convey speed. And if you wanted to describe the effectiveness with which he did moved, you’d use the metaphor, “He tamed the jungle,” despite the entire jungle not being ‘tamed’ thereby.

The media today has taken to use ‘blasted’ to describe the manner in which a politician or other figure merely speaks to his opponents or to the public. But they use it so frequently and about such trifling issues that it has been brought to the point of exhaustion. More than just the exhaustion of the word’s meaning–its incorrect usage renders it free of weight–the word’s overuse incurs exhaustion in the reader. They become desensitized to its use and they desire to stop seeing the word, going so far as to actively avoid reading articles which may use it. And so the media achieves one of their goals–obfuscation of truth–simply by making the act of discovering truth unpalatable to readers.

The media and academia are guilty of killing both the shades of meaning of words, as well as the weight of words themselves. This has caused–entirely purposefully–a serious breakdown in the ability of the members of society to have discourse around a subject if it is deemed particularly sensitive by the people who control the media. The terms white nationalist and Nazi have been treated this way. A national socialist is a white nationalist, but a white nationalist may very well not be a national socialist, since white nationalism is but a single tenet of nationalist socialism, not a completely synonymous term. Conflating words with one another kills gradation. An entire array of words that express a similar–yet cardinally different–concept are all swept under one umbrella term. It is then used exclusively–and overused–to a point at which the word itself feels meaningless, and to the point that most people forget entirely the other gradations for the same meaning.

“It’s a beautiful thing, the destruction of words. Of course the great wastage is in the verbs and adjectives, but there are hundreds of nouns that can be got rid of as well. It isn’t only the synonyms; there are also the antonyms. After all, what justification is there for a word which is simply the opposite of some other word? A word contains its opposite in itself. Take ‘good,’ for instance. If you have a word like ‘good,’ what need is there for a word like ‘bad’? ‘Ungood’ will do just as well–better, because it's an exact opposite, which the other is not. In the end the whole notion of goodness and badness will be covered by only six words–in reality, only one word.” ~ George Orwell; Nineteen Eighty-Four

Points become impossible to argue within a language that has been stripped of its complexity and ambiguity, because the resulting simplicity is what allows people to form black and white narratives about any issue they want. Imagine that a group of white nationalists protested the planned removal of a national monument. If the news reports the group as a “Nazi gathering,” anyone who shows up to oppose the “Nazis” are “counter protesters” and “anti-Nazi,” even if the white nationalists in question are themselves against national socialism. This is a mirror of Nineteen Eighty-Four’s Good/Ungood dichotomy. If you fought against the Ungood, you were automatically Good, because what else can you be, if no words exist to define other concepts? There were only these two things–Good and Ungood–you could have possibly been. No shades, no complex differences, no ambiguity, just Good and Ungood. ‘Nazis’ and ‘Not Nazis.’ If there is anything in language we must actively work to protect, it is the gradation of words. Especially in philosophy or politics, the formation of a false dichotomy is disastrous. Words alone will convince a majority of people the world is made up only of Nazis and “Not Nazis.” Communists, anarchists, and all the rest won’t even exist to them. Even with politics aside, it’s a mark of ignorance and barbarism to use the wrong gradation of a word. It should be embarrassing to confuse words by the weight of their meaning–or by their meanings entirely.

If you shriek and faint at the sight of a cockroach, you shouldn’t say you’re scared of them. In that case, you are terrified. You shouldn’t say you’re annoyed by a neighbor’s dog defecating on your lawn if you’re contemplating killing it in retaliation. In that case, you despise or loathe the dog. You wouldn’t say that getting unjustly evicted is unpleasant, or that the process of said eviction is an inconvenience; you would say it’s terrible or catastrophic or that the process of eviction is an upheaval in your life. You wouldn’t say your daughter dying from cancer is troubling you; you would say it’s unceasingly tormenting you. Use the right words with correct gradation, especially when it comes to subjects of import.

“And, of course, the word love has many shades of meaning, as do many, many of the words in our living, breathing language.” ~ Mary Balogh; Slightly Dangerous, p. 56

One of the beautiful things about the English language is that not a single speaker knows every word of it. Surely you’ve learned at least one new word just from reading this far in this book alone, and not just the words given specific attention by the text. At first glance, this may seem like a bad thing. “Not knowing words” hinders communication. But English uses gradation heavily. Each shade of meaning of a thought, emotion, or action has its own word. With English, we can give a pinpoint reconstruction of a historical event–telling exactly what the people involved did, how they felt, and what resulted thereby–down to its most subtle components.

Such a thing isn’t possible in the languages of Kikuyu or Pirahã, for example. Languages which each speaker knows in full cannot include the complexities of English and other written languages. They must always use the simplest terms (and often eschew entire ideas) because the mind can only remember so much. Gradation isn’t as heavy in their languages, and thus they cannot pinpoint concepts that share similar, core aspects, but have functional differences. You can’t know every word in the English language simply because you cannot know everything there is to express in the language. The vastness in your words is your range of expression. Don’t let simplicity take that away from you. Recall the discussion of both African and Indio languages, and the lack of range afforded therein. Studies on the Pirahã language reveals it has no words for exact numbers. Consequently, they are incapable of accurately counting–or determining quantities–when the numbers are higher than four. Because of the deficiency of the language, the Pirahã people are unable to mentally represent exact numbers greater than three. The limits of their vocabulary determined the limits of their mental concepts.
